questions.text: Migrations are described as being like what?
options: A backup service for your source code
Version control for your database
A template engine for your views
A router for your database queries
questions.explanation: Migrations are like version control for your database, letting your team define and share the application's database schema.

questions.text: Which problem do database migrations solve?
options: Slow page loads caused by uncached routes
Invalid form input being saved to the database
Blade templates not compiling
Having to tell a teammate to manually add a column to their local database after they pull your changes
questions.explanation: If you've ever had to tell a teammate to manually add a column to their local schema after pulling your changes, that's the problem migrations solve.

questions.text: What does the "Consistency" benefit of migrations mean?
options: Every developer has the same database schema, avoiding differences between development, staging and production
Every table uses the same column names
Every query returns results in the same order
Every migration runs at the same time each day
questions.explanation: Migrations make sure all developers have the same schema, avoiding discrepancies between development, staging and production databases.

questions.text: Which benefit of migrations lets you revert the database to its previous state if a migration introduces an issue?
options: Consistency
Collaboration
Rollback Capabilities
Scalability
questions.explanation: Rollback Capabilities: if a migration introduces an issue, rollback commands revert the database to its previous state.

questions.text: Which two tools does the module have you install before creating a migration?
options: Docker and pgAdmin
XAMPP and MySQL Workbench
Node.js and MongoDB Compass
WAMP and phpMyAdmin
questions.explanation: Step 1 is to install XAMPP and MySQL Workbench, then create a MySQL connection and database.

questions.text: What does the up() method of a migration contain?
options: The code that seeds the table with sample data
The code that reverses the migration
The database connection settings
The changes to apply to the database when the migration runs, such as creating tables, adding columns or creating indexes
questions.explanation: up() defines the changes applied when the migration runs: creating tables, adding columns, creating indexes, etc.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the down() method below?
options: It reverses what up() did, so the database can be rolled back
It deletes every table in the database
It runs before up() to prepare the table
It downloads the table's data as a backup
questions.explanation: down() reverses the actions in up() and is used during rollbacks. Here, up() created the personal_access_tokens table, so down() drops it.

questions.text: What does $table->id(); create?
options: A VARCHAR column called id
A UUID column with no primary key
An auto-incrementing primary key (big integer)
An index on an existing id column
questions.explanation: $table->id() creates an auto-incrementing big integer primary key.

questions.text: $table->string('name'); creates a VARCHAR column with what default length?
options: 64 characters
100 characters
191 characters
255 characters
questions.explanation: string() creates a VARCHAR column with a default length of 255 characters. A different length can be passed as the second argument, e.g. string('token', 64).

questions.text: What does $table->float('price', 8, 2); create?
options: A column that stores up to 8 prices
A floating-point column with 8 digits total and 2 decimal places
A floating-point column with 8 decimal places and 2 whole digits
An integer column between 2 and 8
questions.explanation: The second and third arguments are the total digits (8) and decimal places (2).

questions.text: What does the ->nullable() modifier do?
options: Allows the column to accept NULL values, so it isn't required when inserting data
Sets the column's value to NULL for every existing row
Removes the column from the table
Prevents the column from ever being NULL
questions.explanation: ->nullable() lets a column accept NULL values, meaning it isn't required when inserting data.

questions.text: If a row is inserted without a name, what is stored in the name column below?
options: An empty string
NULL
Anonymous
The insert fails with an error
questions.explanation: ->default() sets the value used when none is provided, so the column gets 'Anonymous'. nullable() still allows NULL if you explicitly insert NULL.

questions.text: What does $table->foreignId('user_id')->constrained('users'); do?
options: Creates a new users table
Makes user_id unique across all tables
Copies every user into the current table
Creates a user_id foreign key column connected to the id column of the users table
questions.explanation: foreignId() creates a foreign key column, and constrained('users') connects user_id to the id column of the users table.

questions.text: Following Laravel's recommended naming convention, which model and table pair is correct?
options: Model Product, table products
Model Products, table product
Model product, table Products
Model ProductModel, table ProductTable
questions.explanation: Model names are singular PascalCase (Product, Student), and table names are plural snake_case (products, students).

questions.text: What is the $fillable property of a model used for?
options: It lists the columns that are hidden from JSON output
It sets which database the model connects to
It lists the columns that can be inserted or updated, protecting the app from unwanted data changes
It fills every column with default values
questions.explanation: $fillable lists the columns that can be inserted or updated, which helps protect the application from unwanted data changes.

questions.text: Complete the Artisan command that creates a migration for a products table:
questions.explanation: php artisan make:migration create_products_table creates the migration. (The slide's example is create_product_table; this uses the plural products to follow the module's own table-naming rule.)

questions.text: Complete the Artisan command that creates a model:
questions.explanation: php artisan make:model Product creates a model. Each model typically corresponds to a table in the database.

questions.text: Complete the model property that connects the model to a table whose name doesn't follow Laravel's default naming:
questions.explanation: $table sets the table a model uses. It's needed here because Laravel would otherwise look for a students table.

questions.text: Match each Artisan command to what it does.
allChoices: Rolls back all migrations and then re-runs them
Rolls back the last batch of migrations

pairs.match: Rolls back the last batch of migrations
Rolls back all migrations and then re-runs them

questions.explanation: migrate runs pending migrations; migrate:rollback undoes the last batch; migrate:reset undoes all of them; migrate:refresh undoes all and runs them again. (The slide labels migrate:rollback as "Rollback for a Specific Connection", but on its own it rolls back the last batch — you'd add --database= to target a specific connection.)

questions.text: Match each column method to the column it creates.
allChoices: A TEXT column for longer text

pairs.match: A TEXT column for longer text

questions.explanation: These are the common column types from the module: text, boolean, date, timestamp and json.
